report.source_text: The patient was admitted to the hospital for further management. Intravenous hydration and subcutaneous basal and prandial insulin were administered. Serum blood glucose levels normalised over the next 24–48 hours. Severe hemichorea-hemiballismus persisted, which impaired his ambulation and sleep. Due to severe insomnia and overnight agitation, the patient was initially treated with escalating doses of olanzapine. Low-dose clonazepam was added to the regimen on day 3 hospitalisation with minimal improvement. On day 4 olanzapine was stopped and risperidone 2 mg nightly was started with improvement in both sleep and right arm and right leg chorea-hemiballismus. The patient’s clinical symptoms of hemichorea-hemiballismus were markedly improved prior to discharge on hospital day 6.

report.source_text: He was discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility with subcutaneous insulin, sitagliptin and risperidone with plans for ambulatory follow-up with endocrinology and neurology. The patient completed a successful course of acute rehabilitation following hospital discharge. Two months post-hospitalisation the intensity and frequency of the patient’s hemichorea involving the right upper and lower extremity had decreased and he had returned to all his usual activities. At 6-month follow-up, mild chorea in his right arm persisted.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An elderly man with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes presented with sudden onset right-sided hemichorea and hemiballismus. Initial workup revealed severe hyperglycemia (597 mg/dL) and acute on chronic kidney injury. Brain imaging (CT and MRI) showed characteristic findings of basal ganglia abnormality (hyperdensity in left lentiform and caudate nucleus on CT, increased T1 signal in left putamen on MRI) with sparing of the internal capsule, and no evidence of acute stroke. The patient was admitted, and blood glucose levels normalized within 24-48 hours with insulin and hydration. The movement disorder persisted initially but showed marked improvement by hospital day 6 with symptomatic treatment (risperidone). At 2-month follow-up, the intensity and frequency of hemichorea had decreased, and the patient returned to usual activities. Mild chorea in the right arm persisted at 6-month follow-up.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with sudden onset right-sided choreiform and flinging movements (hemichorea/hemiballismus).
Patient had severe hyperglycemia with a blood glucose level of 597 mg/dL.
CT scan showed faint hyperdensity involving the left lentiform nucleus and caudate nucleus.
MRI showed an increased T1 signal intensity in the putamen on the left.
Radiological findings included basal ganglia abnormality with the sparing of the internal capsule.
Blood glucose levels normalized over 24-48 hours with treatment.
Hemichorea-hemiballismus markedly improved prior to discharge and continued to improve at 2-month follow-up, with mild chorea persisting at 6 months.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: MRI did not demonstrate evidence of acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke (E002).
